# Working with Dates

## Overview
At some point in time (:p), you'll need to work with date data. Dates look simple when displayed, but internally they must carry a real date or date-time class before R can sort, subtract, group, or plot them reliably.

This chapter shows how to construct dates, extract calendar features such as month and weekday, flag dates that satisfy a rule, summarize recurring events, and calculate dates relative to a reference point.

## Load libs

The tidyverse handles transformation and plotting; the lubridate functions used below make parsing and extracting date components more readable.
```r
library(tidyverse)
```

```r
# create date matrix
df <- expand.grid(month=seq(1,12,1),
                  day=seq(1,31,1),
                  year=seq(1930,2030)) %>%
  mutate(mdy = lubridate::mdy(paste0(month,"/",day,"/",year))) %>%
  mutate(dt_month = lubridate::month(mdy),
         dt_day = lubridate::day(mdy),
         dt_year = lubridate::year(mdy),
         dt_week = lubridate::week(mdy),
         dt_yday = lubridate::yday(mdy),
         dt_weekday = lubridate::wday(mdy),
         dt_weekday_l = lubridate::wday(mdy, label=T)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(dt_weekday)) # remove feb 29, 30, 31

knitr::kable(head(df))

```

The grid intentionally includes impossible dates such as February 30. `mdy()` converts those combinations to missing values, and the final filter removes them. This illustrates why validating parsed dates is part of data cleaning.

```r

# mark specific dates
df_marked <- df %>%
  mutate(cinco_de_mayo_taco_tuesday = ifelse(dt_month == 5 &
                                dt_day == 5 &
                                dt_weekday_l == "Tue", 1, 0),
         friday_13th = ifelse(dt_day == 13 &
                                dt_weekday_l == "Fri", 1, 0),
         erica_bday = ifelse(dt_day == 4 &
                               dt_month == 4, 1, 0))

# segment days Alexa mentioned
all_cinco_de_mayo_taco_tuesday <- df_marked %>%
  filter(cinco_de_mayo_taco_tuesday == 1)

all_friday13th <- df_marked %>%
  filter(friday_13th == 1)

all_erica <- df_marked %>%
  filter(erica_bday == 1) %>%
  filter(year >= 1991)

```

Each indicator expresses a calendar rule as a logical condition. Separating the rule definition from later filtering makes the analysis easier to audit and extend.

## Count wife birthday by day of week

Once dates have labeled weekdays, an ordinary grouped count answers a calendar question. The same pattern works for appointment attendance, daily diary completion, or events recorded by day of week.
```r
erica_wkday <- all_erica %>%
  group_by(dt_weekday_l) %>%
  summarise(n = n())

```

## Plot time series of Cinco de Mayo landing on a Tuesday (Taco Tuesday!)

Different geometries emphasize different aspects of the same data. Tiles highlight which years meet the condition; paths emphasize recurrence over time; bars summarize frequency by category.

```r
ggplot(df_marked, aes(year, cinco_de_mayo_taco_tuesday)) +
  geom_tile() +
  theme_minimal()

ggplot(df_marked, aes(year, cinco_de_mayo_taco_tuesday)) +
  geom_path() +
  theme_minimal()

ggplot(erica_wkday, aes(dt_weekday_l, n, group=dt_weekday_l, fill=dt_weekday_l)) +
  geom_bar(stat="identity")
```

## Calculating dates relative to other dates

::: {.callout-important title="Use real date types"}

These operations work on types as.Date data types (and related as.POSIXct), not character data.

:::

```r
ref_date = as.Date("2020-10-11")
paste0("Reference date: ", ref_date)
paste0("Reference date - 90 days: ", ref_date - 90)
paste0("Reference date + 90 days: ", ref_date + 90)
```

## Takeaways

Parse character values into real date classes early, check for failed conversions, and derive calendar features only after parsing. Once dates are represented correctly, filtering, grouping, arithmetic, and visualization use the same grammar as other tidy data operations.
